title: Tannat
description: The most tannic grape of south-west France, which found a softer second home in Uruguay.
L: A grape named for its grip
Describe Tannat's colour, tannin and flavours

Tannat is a black grape from south-west France, near the Pyrenees. Its name likely comes from the same root as tannin, and it has more than almost any other grape. In the glass it is deep purple, almost black, with blackberry, plum, liquorice and smoky, spicy notes. Acidity is high too.
Very high tannin, very dark colour

Tannat has small berries with thick skins, and unusually many seeds: often five per berry, where most grapes have two to three. Skins and seeds both carry tannin. Tannat is also very rich in procyanidins, a family of antioxidant compounds, and studies have found it among the highest of all red grapes.
Why does Tannat have so much tannin?
Its berries have thick skins and many seeds
It is blended with white grapes
Tannin comes from skins and seeds. Tannat has thick skins and often five seeds per berry.

A young Tannat is almost opaque, with a purple rim. On the palate, the tannin grips the gums firmly, more than Cabernet Sauvignon. The fruit is dark, the finish often slightly bitter and spicy. With a few years in bottle, the tannins soften and leather and tobacco notes appear.
A young Tannat usually has more tannin than a young Cabernet Sauvignon.
Yes. Tannat is one of the most tannic grapes in the world, firmer than most Cabernet.
Tannat is very dark and very tannic, with high acidity
Thick skins and many seeds give it that grip
It shows blackberry, liquorice and smoke, softening with age
The Pyrenees and the River Plate
Compare the climates of both homes

Tannat's French home is Madiran, in Gascony, close to the Pyrenees. Madiran must be at least 60% Tannat, often blended with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon or Fer Servadou. The climate is mild and fairly wet, with Atlantic influence. Tannat also appears in Irouléguy, in the Basque Country, and in Saint-Mont.

Basque immigrants brought Tannat to Uruguay in the 1870s; one of them, Pascual Harriague, gave it its early local name, Harriague. Today it is Uruguay's national grape, about a quarter of the vineyard. Uruguay's humid, maritime climate on the River Plate and the Atlantic gives Tannat riper, rounder tannins than in Madiran.
Match each place to its Tannat connection.
Tannat travelled from the Basque Country to South America with emigrants.

Both homes are humid, with rain during the growing season, unlike the dry Andes. Growers must fight disease. Uruguay is warmer and gets more sun, so Tannat ripens more fully. Canelones, near Montevideo, makes most of it; Maldonado, near the sea, and Rivera, in the north, give new styles.
Why is Tannat from Uruguay often softer than Madiran?
It is made from different grapes
Uruguay's warmer, sunnier climate ripens the tannins more
It is blended with white wine
More warmth and sun bring riper, rounder tannins.
Madiran, near the Pyrenees, is Tannat's French home
Basque immigrants took it to Uruguay in the 1870s
Uruguay's warmer climate gives softer, riper Tannat
Describe other ways to soften Tannat

In 1991, Madiran winemaker Patrick Ducournau developed micro-oxygenation: tiny, controlled doses of oxygen bubbled into the wine. It helps tannins link into longer chains, which feel softer, and stabilises colour. Born to tame Tannat, the technique is now used all over the world.

Winemakers also soften Tannat by picking when skins and seeds are fully ripe, by gentle extraction, avoiding crushed seeds, by shorter maceration and by ageing in oak, where slow oxygen through the wood helps. In Uruguay, some producers make lighter, fresher Tannat with little oak to drink young.
What does micro-oxygenation do to Tannat?
Helps tannins soften and stabilises colour
Small, controlled doses of oxygen help tannins polymerise, so they feel softer, and fix colour.

Blending is the oldest solution. In Madiran, Cabernet Franc adds perfume and lightness. In Uruguay, Tannat is often blended with Merlot or Pinot Noir to soften it, or with Marselan. Some producers even co-ferment a little white Viognier, adding aroma and helping colour.
Crushing seeds releases harsh tannin, the opposite of what you want.
Micro-oxygenation was invented in Madiran in 1991 for Tannat
Ripe picking, gentle extraction and oak soften it
Blending with Cabernet Franc or Merlot adds softness

Tannin binds to fat and protein, so Tannat shines with rich meat. In Uruguay, it's the wine of the asado, beef grilled slowly over wood. In Gascony, it goes with duck confit and cassoulet. The fat softens the tannin; the tannin cleans the palate.

Serve Tannat at 16 to 18 degrees. Young, powerful examples benefit from decanting for an hour or two. Good Madiran can age 10 to 20 years, when the tannins soften and earthy, leather notes emerge. Lighter Uruguayan styles are best within a few years.
Decant young; good Madiran ages 10 to 20 years
Which dish suits a young Tannat best?
Fatty grilled meat softens Tannat's tannin. Delicate fish would taste metallic next to it.
Uruguay's sweet fortified Tannat, sometimes called Tannat licoroso, is a good match for dark chocolate.
Tannat is best served very cold, like a white wine.
Not true. Cold makes tannin feel harsher. Serve it at 16 to 18 degrees.
Tannat loves fatty, grilled meat and duck
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, and decant when young
Good Madiran ages for 10 to 20 years
